readerTitle: The poster said speak up. The kitchen said otherwise.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 주방, 대기업 안의 IT 운영팀) + 실제 기업·연구 (NUMMI 공장, John Shook의 글, Edgar Schein의 문화 형성 이론)
insight: 문화는 선언으로 바뀌지 않는다. 사람들이 반복해서 보는 작은 순간, 즉 어떤 행동 뒤에 무슨 일이 일어나는지를 바꾸면 생각은 뒤따라 바뀐다.
misconception: 새 가치를 발표하고 교육하고 포스터를 붙이면 문화가 바뀐다. 사람들의 생각이 먼저 바뀌어야 행동이 바뀐다.

sources.text: Shook, J. (2010). How to Change a Culture: Lessons From NUMMI. MIT Sloan Management Review, 51(2).
Schein, E. H. Organizational Culture and Leadership (리더가 주의를 기울이는 것, 위기 대응, 보상 배분 등 문화 형성 메커니즘)
레스토랑과 IT 운영팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: NUMMI: GM 프리몬트 공장은 1982년 문을 닫았고, 1984년 GM-토요타 합작사 NUMMI로 재가동되며 상당수 기존 노조 노동자를 다시 고용했습니다. 몇 년 안에 품질이 GM 공장 중 최상위권이 되었다는 내용은 Shook(2010)에 근거합니다. 게시 전 원문으로 연도와 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
Shook의 핵심 주장(생각을 바꿔 행동을 바꾸기보다 행동을 바꿔 생각을 바꾸는 편이 쉽다)은 카드에서 직접 인용하지 않고 풀어 썼습니다. 정확한 인용문을 쓰려면 원문 확인이 필요합니다.
Schein의 메커니즘 목록은 저서마다 표현이 조금 다릅니다. 카드에서는 '리더가 주목하는 것, 위기 때의 반응, 보상과 승진' 세 가지만 일반적으로 언급했습니다.

cards.title: The poster said speak up. The kitchen said otherwise.
body: After a near miss with undercooked chicken, a restaurant owner hangs a new sign by the pass: *We speak up about problems.*
Friday, 8 p.m., a full dining room. A line cook says the walk-in fridge feels warm. The head chef snaps, "Not now." Everyone hears it.
The sign stays on the wall. But the whole team just learned the real rule.

image.label: Busy kitchen with a 'speak up' sign and a cook being waved off
image.brief: 바쁜 레스토랑 주방. 벽에 "We speak up about problems" 포스터. 앞쪽에서 셰프가 손을 들어 젊은 요리사의 말을 막고, 다른 직원들이 곁눈질로 지켜봄. 따뜻한 조명, 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: You own the restaurant. How do you make speaking up normal?
body: Your staff stay quiet about problems because, in the past, raising one during service got them yelled at. You want that to change. Where do you start?

options.text: Hold a staff meeting on why speaking up matters, then run a short training
options.feedback: It explains the goal clearly, but people trust what happens on a Friday night more than what's said in a meeting. If the reaction stays the same, the training gets ignored.

options.text: Change what happens right after someone raises a problem: thank them on the spot and fix it that shift, starting with you and the head chef
options.feedback: This changes the moment staff actually remember. It takes repetition, and the head chef has to buy in, but each good reaction is evidence the rule is real.

options.text: Replace the head chef with someone calmer
options.feedback: It sends a strong signal and may be needed. But a new chef walks into the same habits, and without a new routine the old silence can survive the change.

cards.title: The owner changed one 30-second moment.
body: The owner and head chef agreed on a simple response. When anyone flags a problem, even mid-rush, the answer is "Thanks, good catch," and someone deals with it before close.
They also added one question to the two-minute pre-shift huddle: *What almost went wrong yesterday?* The owner answered first, with her own mistake.
The first weeks were awkward. Then a dishwasher reported a leaking gas hose. He was thanked in front of everyone. After that, reports came more often.

cards.title: Culture changes when the consequences change
body: Culture is the set of unwritten rules people learn by watching what happens. To **change a culture**, change what people do and what follows when they do it. New beliefs come after the new experience, not before.
That's why announcements rarely work on their own. People don't ask "What did the boss say?" They ask "What happened to the last person who tried this?"

image.label: Old loop vs new loop: action, reaction, lesson learned
image.brief: 두 개의 순환 고리 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Old loop": Raise a problem → Get snapped at → Stay quiet. 오른쪽 "New loop": Raise a problem → Get thanked, it gets fixed → Speak up again. 오른쪽 고리를 밝은 색으로 강조.

cards.title: Same workers, different system.
body: GM's Fremont car plant had a reputation for poor quality and was closed in 1982. It reopened in 1984 as NUMMI, a joint venture with Toyota, and rehired many of the same workers.

According to John Shook, a manager who helped set it up, quality soon rose to among the best in GM. Toyota didn't start by changing minds. It changed daily work, such as letting any worker stop the line to fix a problem, and backed them when they did.
Researcher Edgar Schein points to the same levers: what leaders pay attention to, how they react in a crisis, and who gets rewarded.

cards.title: Change is slow, and one slip resets it.
body: People test a new rule many times before they trust it. One angry reaction from a leader under pressure can undo weeks of good ones.
Systems can also quietly fight you. If pay, promotions or targets still reward the old behavior, the old behavior wins.
So pick one or two behaviors, not ten. Make sure leaders model them first, and check that rewards point the same way.

cards.title: Now it's an IT team inside a bank.
body: You've just taken over an IT operations team. Here, heroes fix outages at 2 a.m. and get praised in leadership emails. Nobody notices the quiet work that prevents outages. You want prevention to become the norm. What's your first move?

options.text: Send a team email: "From now on, we value prevention over firefighting"
options.feedback: It's clear and costs nothing. But if the 2 a.m. fix still earns the praise, people will believe the praise, not the email.

options.text: In each weekly review, spotlight the fix that prevented an incident, stop celebrating all-nighters, and add prevention work to team goals
options.feedback: This changes what gets noticed and rewarded, which is what people watch. It takes months, and you'll need your own boss to stop praising the heroics too.

options.text: Ban after-hours work except for real emergencies
options.feedback: It removes a visible symptom. But if the outages and the rewards don't change, late work may just go unreported.

cards.title: Change the moment, and the belief follows.
body: Culture shifts when people see a new behavior lead to a better outcome, again and again, starting with the leaders.
**Try it today:** pick one behavior you want more of. Write down what currently happens right after someone does it. What would you change about that reaction?
